findings.quote: Use [aws:SourceVpce](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-source-vpce-condition) with an endpoint in a **virtual private cloud** (vee-pee-SEE), or VPC, instead.
findings.evidence: The 'Spot the bug' fix repeats the bug. A Deny on requests that do not come from one VPC endpoint denies the rotation function too, unless that function runs in the VPC and calls Secrets Manager through that endpoint; AWS gives the same warning for aws:SourceVpc/aws:SourceVpce as for aws:SourceIp. Source docs/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/best-practices (Limit requests with VPC endpoint conditions): "If you use these condition keys in a resource policy statement that allows or denies access to Secrets Manager secrets, you can inadvertently deny access to services that use Secrets Manager to access secrets on your behalf. Only some AWS services can run with an endpoint within your VPC. If you restrict requests for a secret to a VPC or VPC endpoint, then calls to Secrets Manager from a service not configured for the service can fail." The reader would copy a policy that still breaks rotation (and, with Principal "*" and secretsmanager:*, also blocks administrators outside the endpoint from changing the policy). Fix: 'Use aws:SourceVpce only if the rotation function runs in the VPC and calls Secrets Manager through that endpoint (see the interface endpoint in Go deeper); otherwise scope the Deny so that it does not match the rotation function.' Needs a fact from the quote above.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The answer no longer offers aws:SourceVpce as the fix. It reads 'A Deny on [aws:SourceVpce] has the same risk: [you can inadvertently deny access to services](secrets-manager-vpc-condition-can-block-services).' (verified fact from the best-practices quote).

findings.quote: "kills": "\"A SecureString parameter returns its plain value to anyone who calls GetParameter.\""
findings.evidence: The task 'kills' a belief that is in practice true for the setup it builds. Step 2 uses the default key aws/ssm, and that key gives kms:Decrypt to every IAM principal in the account, so anyone allowed ssm:GetParameter gets the plain value by adding --with-decryption (step 4). The break-it step (step 3) shows only that the default response is encrypted, and the reader learns a false sense of access control. Source docs/systems-manager/latest/userguide/parameter-store-setting-up (Denying permissions, Note): "The default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key has `Decrypt` permission for all IAM principals within the AWS account. If you want different access levels to `SecureString` parameters in your account, we don't recommend that you use the default key. Restricting `kms:Decrypt` on a customer managed key prevents decryption of a `SecureString` value through any retrieval operation." The task's permissions list also omits kms:Decrypt, which works only because of this default-key behavior. Fix: rewrite 'kills' as 'WithDecryption is a security control', and add to the step 4 explain: 'With aws/ssm, every principal that can call GetParameter can decrypt; to limit who reads the value, use a customer managed key and grant kms:Decrypt narrowly.' Needs a fact from the quote above.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): kills now reads '"Leaving out WithDecryption hides a SecureString value from the people who can call GetParameter."' Step 3 explain adds 'The flag is a request option, not a permission: the reader needs kms:Decrypt [regardless of which Parameter Store operation is used](parameter-store-securestring-needs-kms-decrypt).' Step 4 text: 'as the same caller ... No extra permission was added.' The aws/ssm 'Decrypt permission for all IAM principals' sentence is not stated: it is in the corpus (docs/systems-manager/latest/userguide/parameter-store-setting-up, line 122) but no verified fact holds it. For the registrar: mine that sentence for chapter 07.

findings.quote: The reader needs kms:Decrypt [regardless of which Parameter Store operation is used](../facts/parameter-store.md#parameter-store-securestring-needs-kms-decrypt).
findings.evidence: The sentence comes right after step 3, which teaches the default key aws/ssm. Read together, they suggest that kms:Decrypt limits who can read a SecureString; with aws/ssm it does not, because that key already allows Decrypt for every principal in the account. Source docs/systems-manager/latest/userguide/parameter-store-setting-up (Note): "The default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key has `Decrypt` permission for all IAM principals within the AWS account. Exam relevance (Domain 1, the reader's weakest): 'restrict which roles can read a SecureString' is answered by a customer managed key with a narrow key policy, not by aws/ssm. Fix: add 'With aws/ssm every principal in the account has it; to restrict readers, use a customer managed key.' Related to technical-02.

findings.quote: 2. **CloudFront to the load balancer.** You can [import the certificate in any AWS Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region) for the origin.
findings.evidence: Out of context the display says the reverse of the section's rule. The CloudFront sentence means only that CloudFront does not force the origin certificate into us-east-1; the load balancer still needs a certificate in its own Region. Verified fact acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource: "ACM certificates must be in the same Region as the resource where they are being used." The table three lines lower says 'Its own: it must be in the same Region', so the step and the table disagree for a reader who skims. Fix: 'CloudFront to the load balancer. The certificate stays in the load balancer's Region: CloudFront does not need it in us-east-1.' and link the display 'must be in the same Region'.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Step 2 now reads 'The origin certificate [must be in the same Region](acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.'

findings.quote: The load balancer keeps its eu-west-1 certificate, because you can [import the certificate in any AWS Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region) for the origin.
findings.evidence: Wrong reason, same root cause as technical-06 (5-quiz.md Question 3, Why). The load balancer keeps its eu-west-1 certificate because an ACM certificate must be in the Region of the resource that uses it, and the load balancer is in eu-west-1. Fact acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource: "ACM certificates must be in the same Region as the resource where they are being used." and "The only exception is Amazon CloudFront, a global service that requires certificates in the US East (N. Virginia) region." Fix: 'The load balancer keeps its eu-west-1 certificate, because a load balancer's certificate [must be in the same Region](...).'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Done as suggested (explanation only; stem, options and key unchanged, so no new verification). q002 facts now list acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource instead of acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region.

findings.quote: a rotated password reaches the application on its next read. The code change is one SDK call, and [using a cache can reduce your costs](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-cache-cost-latency) and latency.
findings.evidence: The correct option reads the secret 'through a cache', and the Why (5-quiz.md Question 1) and 2-deep.md ('so the next read gets the new password', next to 'A cache (KASH) helps') say the new password arrives on the next read. With the AWS caching component, a cached value is refreshed on a timer and is not invalidated by a rotation, and single-user rotation has a short window of denied calls. Source docs/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/retrieving-secrets_cache-python: "By default, the cache refreshes secrets every hour." and "The cache implementation does not include cache invalidation." Source docs/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotation-strategy: "During this time, there is a low risk of the database denying calls that use the rotated credentials. You can mitigate this risk with an appropriate retry strategy." An application built as described can fail new connections for up to an hour after a rotation. Fix: 'a rotated password reaches the application at the next cache refresh; on an authentication error, the application reads the secret again', and the same in 2-deep 'Why a call?'. Needs facts from the quotes above.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): q003 explanation now says 'a rotation needs no deployment', then 'A cached value changes at the next refresh: for the Python caching client, [By default, the cache refreshes secrets every hour](secrets-manager-cache-refresh-hourly-default). After a failed login, the application reads the secret again.' Option d why: 'at the next read from Secrets Manager'. Worked step 6: 'when it next reads the secret'. Option texts, stem and key unchanged. 2-deep 'Why a call?' says 'the next read from Secrets Manager', and the Decision record Trade-off says the application retries its connection after a rotation.

findings.evidence: The question asks which service can rotate the key; the answer cites a fact about storing kinds of secrets, and implies that rotation of a third-party API key is built in. Except for listed partner integrations (managed external secrets), Secrets Manager rotates such a key only through a rotation function that you write. Verified fact secrets-manager-faq-custom-rotation-lambda: "You can extend Secrets Manager to rotate other secrets, such as credentials for Oracle databases hosted on EC2 or custom applications generating tokens, by modifying sample AWS Lambda functions available in the Secrets Manager documentation." Fix: 'Secrets Manager, with a rotation function that you write [by modifying sample AWS Lambda functions](...); Parameter Store cannot rotate it.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Check 2 answer now reads 'Secrets Manager: you write the rotation function [by modifying sample AWS Lambda functions](secrets-manager-faq-custom-rotation-lambda).' Predict 2 keeps 'its credential rotation is [None]'.

findings.quote: Secrets Manager rotates the password with a Lambda function.
findings.evidence: The chapter teaches managed rotation (2-deep 'Automatic rotation...': RDS rotates the master user secret without a Lambda function; the Stop-and-answer there says the old Lambda function is not called). The spoken answer says rotation always uses Lambda, and the reader would tell a CTO with RDS to build a function. Verified fact secrets-manager-managed-rotation-no-lambda: "With managed rotation, you don't use an AWS Lambda function to update the secret and the credentials in the database." Fix: 'Secrets Manager rotates the password for you: Amazon RDS can manage it, and other databases use a rotation function.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): s01 line 5 now reads 'Secrets Manager rotates the password. For Amazon RDS, RDS can manage that for you.' (managed rotation facts added to s01).

findings.quote: **Stop and answer.** PutParameter fails for a 6 KB JSON document of feature flags as a standard parameter. What is the cheapest fix?
findings.evidence: The answer 'An advanced parameter' is not the cheapest fix: two standard parameters of 3 KB each have no storage charge, while an advanced parameter costs $0.05 per month (verified fact parameter-store-price-advanced-parameter: 'No additional charge' for standard, '$0.05 per advanced parameter per month'). The stem also uses feature flags, which AWS places in AWS AppConfig, not Parameter Store. Source docs/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store (comparison table, Typical data): Parameter Store "Approved AMI IDs ... Endpoint URLs"; AWS AppConfig "Feature flags". Fix: ask 'What is the simplest fix that keeps one parameter?' and use a non-flag value (for example a 6 KB certificate chain or JSON settings document).
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The Stop and answer now reads 'PutParameter fails for a 6 KB JSON settings document as a standard parameter. What is the simplest fix that keeps one parameter?'

findings.quote: 4. **Delete.** A deleted secret waits [from 7 to 30](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-recovery-window-range) days
findings.evidence: Stated as unconditional. The verified fact's scope says 'ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery skips the window', and the default is 30 days. Source docs/secretsmanager/latest/apireference/API_DeleteSecret: "If you don't use either, then by default Secrets Manager uses a 30 day recovery window." and "If you delete a secret with the `ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery` parameter, then you have no opportunity to recover the secret. You lose the secret permanently." Card c003 repeats the unconditional form. Fix: 'A deleted secret waits 30 days by default (you can choose from 7 to 30), unless the call forces deletion without recovery.' Needs a fact for the default and the force option.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Step 4 now adds 'A forced delete leaves [no opportunity to recover the secret](secrets-manager-force-delete-without-recovery).' The 30-day default is not added (word cap). Card c003 ('the recovery window of a deleted secret ... runs from 7 to 30') describes the window itself, so it stays true.

findings.quote: The exception is a secret that Amazon ECS injects at task start: [you must force a new deployment](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-ecs-redeploy-for-new-value) or launch a new task.

Fact secrets-manager-ecs-redeploy-for-new-value covers ECS only. Fix: 'The exception is any value read only at start, for example a secret that Amazon ECS injects at task start: ...'.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The Exam trap now reads 'A value read at start is the exception: for Amazon ECS, [you must force a new deployment] or launch a new task.'

findings.quote: **Requirement.** The database password must rotate every 30 days with no downtime and no new deployment, with the LEAST operational overhead.
findings.evidence: The decision meets 'no downtime' only with retries or the alternating-users strategy; the default single-user strategy has a short window of denied calls. Source docs/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotation-strategy: "While rotation is happening, there is a low risk of the database denying calls that use the rotated credentials. You can mitigate this risk with an appropriate retry strategy." Verified fact secrets-manager-alternating-users-high-availability: "applications that require high availability". Fix: in Trade-off, 'reconnects with retries after a rotation, or uses alternating-users rotation'.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The Trade-off now ends 'The application retries its connection after a rotation.'
